name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,127

clue.text: Prudent, being consumed by worry?

blocks.note: first meaning: cautious and sensible
second meaning, read literally: full of care, an old sense of the word meaning anxious

explanation.surface: Someone sensible because they are eaten up with anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as CARE-FUL: full of care. The older sense of the word was 'anxious', which the second half of the clue spells out.
explanation.definitionFit: A cautious, sensible person takes pains to avoid risk; the archaic sense meant troubled and anxious.

clue.text: Armistice broken by Charlie Potter

indicators.note: something broken is smashed into bits, so the letters of the treaty word are scattered and rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A truce violated by someone named Charlie Potter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie Potter' reads as a person's name, but Charlie is the letter C added to the fodder and Potter is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A potter shapes clay into pots and other fired pieces, which is exactly a ceramics worker's craft.

clue.text: Mat to hand for sport

blocks.note: a rug is a small mat
close by, near to hand

explanation.surface: A mat kept handy for some athletic activity.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugby is a team game played with an oval ball, one specific example of a sport.

clue.text: Close relative in Highland dance showing off

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, so the relative goes within the dance

blocks.note: an aunt is a close family member
the Highland fling is a lively Scottish dance

explanation.surface: An aunt or similar performing a Scottish dance and making a display of herself.
explanation.walkthrough: The Highland fling is a traditional Scottish solo dance.
explanation.definitionFit: To flaunt is to display something ostentatiously, so the present participle matches parading oneself.

clue.text: Refuse group of newborn

blocks.note: first meaning: rubbish dropped about, read as the noun REF-use
second meaning: the young born to an animal at one time

explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like the verb to decline, but it is the noun meaning rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Discarded rubbish strewn around is one sense; a set of puppies or kittens born together is the other.

clue.text: Plunder big bag

blocks.note: first meaning: to pillage a captured town
second meaning: a large coarse bag for goods

explanation.surface: Looting with a large bag to carry the spoils.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers who pillage a town are said to do this to it, and a large coarse bag carries potatoes or coal.

clue.text: Juice: nothing odd in usual power

indicators.note: with no odd-placed letters kept, only the second and fourth letters of the following word survive

blocks.note: the even letters of this word
P is the symbol for power in physics

explanation.surface: A note that a drink has no oddities in its normal strength.
explanation.definitionFit: Sap is the fluid circulating in a plant, a natural liquid comparable to fruit juice.

clue.text: Panic at changing leader

indicators.note: changing means altering the order, so the letters of the first two words are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Fear spreading at a change of boss.
explanation.definitionFit: A captain heads a team or commands a ship, so is a leader of a group.

clue.text: From the start relish a good scrap

indicators.note: taking from the start of each word means using only their opening letters

blocks.note: the first letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Someone who enjoys a decent fight right from the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' suggests a fight, but here it is a scrap of cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A rag is a small torn piece of cloth, so a scrap of fabric.

clue.text: A new bit of advice: work with energy for unrecognised leader

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
a tip is a helpful hint
op is short for opus, a work
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A fresh hint: put effort into backing a leader nobody acknowledges.
explanation.walkthrough: OP for opus (a musical work) is a standard crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An antipope claimed the papacy in opposition to the canonically elected pontiff, so the Church did not accept him.

clue.text: Write feeble second half of letter in verse

definitions.note: the answer is a metre of verse rather than verse itself

indicators.note: only the back half of the following word is kept, its first half discarded

blocks.note: to pen is to write
tame means dull or weak
the back three of its six letters

explanation.surface: Instructions to compose the weak end of a letter as a poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Pentameter is a line of five metrical feet, the standard measure of much English poetry such as Shakespeare's.

clue.text: Old Central American person hides always

indicators.note: something that hides another keeps it tucked inside, so the person wraps around the word for always

blocks.note: a man is a person
ay (or aye) is an old word for always

explanation.surface: An ancient American who is forever in hiding.
explanation.walkthrough: AY meaning ever or always is archaic, surviving in 'for aye'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Maya were the ancient civilisation of Mexico, Guatemala and Belize, so one of them is from that region's past.

clue.text: Hug me back: steady!

indicators.note: going back means running the preceding short word from end to start

blocks.note: taken as written
to brace is to steady or support

explanation.surface: A plea to be hugged in return, then a call to hold firm.
explanation.definitionFit: To embrace someone is to wrap your arms around them in a hug, the same action expressed as a verb.

clue.text: Sign to leave miserable apostle

blocks.note: feeling blue is feeling sad
Peter was one of the twelve apostles

explanation.surface: A notice telling a gloomy disciple to go.
explanation.walkthrough: The Blue Peter is a blue flag with a white square, hoisted when a ship is about to sail.
explanation.definitionFit: This naval signal flag tells crew and shore that the vessel is about to depart port.

clue.text: Where knockout is likely, put ice out

indicators.note: out here means out of order, so the letters are put into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to apply ice where a boxer is likely to be flattened.
explanation.walkthrough: A cup tie is a match in a knockout cup competition, as in English football's FA Cup; 'knockout' suggests boxing.
explanation.definitionFit: In a cup competition the loser of each match is eliminated, so knockout is the format of such a fixture.

clue.text: Demonstrate in favour of trial

blocks.note: pro means for or supporting
a test is a trial

explanation.surface: Showing that you support putting something on trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demonstrate' looks like 'show', but here it means to march or rally against something.
explanation.definitionFit: To demonstrate in the political sense is to march or rally publicly to object, which is to protest.

clue.text: Turning up, mean at last to score basket

indicators.note: turning the next short word round makes it run the other way
at last points to the final letter only of the preceding word

blocks.note: taken as written
its final letter
to net is to score a goal

explanation.surface: A stingy person finally turning up to score a goal in basketball.
explanation.walkthrough: A punnet is a small square basket or box for soft fruit such as strawberries, a common British word.
explanation.definitionFit: Shop strawberries and raspberries come in these small light containers, a kind of fruit basket.

clue.text: Request recording of a cascade of bells

indicators.note: a recording captures sound, so what counts is how the words are heard, not spelt

blocks.note: a peal is a ringing sequence of bells

explanation.surface: Asking for a recording of church bells ringing out.
explanation.definitionFit: An appeal is an earnest plea or call for help or money, so a request.

clue.text: Temporary fix as apps got confused

indicators.note: becoming confused means getting mixed up, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; it doubles as part of the indicator phrase

explanation.surface: A quick workaround needed because some phone applications malfunctioned.
explanation.definitionFit: A stopgap is a makeshift measure used until something permanent replaces it, so a short-term remedy.

clue.text: Saint breaks into type of Sunday hymn

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so the saint goes within the other word

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for saint
Palm Sunday is the Sunday before Easter

explanation.surface: A holy figure bursts in on a particular Sunday's hymn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type of Sunday hymn' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'hymn'.
explanation.definitionFit: The psalms are the sacred songs of the Book of Psalms, sung in worship as hymns.

clue.text: Make embarrassed in a party

blocks.note: taken as written
a bash is a lively party

explanation.surface: Being made to feel awkward at a social gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: To abash someone is to make them feel ashamed or self-conscious, so to cause discomfort and blushes.

clue.text: Once more grab time off, trailing back

indicators.note: trailing means following behind, so the time-off word comes after the other one

blocks.note: the rear is the back
a rest is a break from work

explanation.surface: Taking another break, lagging behind the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grab' here means to arrest, as police grab a suspect.
explanation.definitionFit: Police who arrest a suspect a second time detain them again, taking hold of them once more.

clue.text: Polish most of gemstone

indicators.note: most of means not all, so the last letter of the stone's name is dropped

blocks.note: a ruby is a red precious stone

explanation.surface: Buffing up a large part of a jewel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' could be the nationality, but here it is the verb to shine.
explanation.definitionFit: To polish a surface you work a cloth across it with friction, so the verb to buff or shine.

clue.text: Perhaps member of army finishing lieutenant

indicators.note: the finishing part of a word is its tail, so only the closing letters are used

blocks.note: its last three letters

explanation.surface: Possibly a soldier who ends up a lieutenant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Army' suggests soldiers, but army ants march in huge colonies, so one insect is a member of an army.
explanation.definitionFit: Army ants are a group of insects that forage in vast columns, so one such insect belongs to an army.

clue.text: Go and return potty

indicators.note: to return is to come back the way you went, so the word is read from its end

blocks.note: bats means crazy

explanation.surface: An instruction to leave and come back to the toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potty' looks like a child's toilet, but here it means mad; 'Go' is the noun, as in have a go.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a go at something is making an attempt, and so is having a stab at it.

clue.text: Unsteady dog?

blocks.note: surface reading: a hound that wobbles on its legs
setter's reading: a breed of dog whose name also describes anyone who staggers or sways

explanation.walkthrough: The name of a crossbred hunting dog, popular in Britain, also means one who lurches.
explanation.definitionFit: This crossbreed of greyhound and collie or terrier is a dog, and someone who staggers about lurches.
